newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU veto rule blamed for Danish move on Cuba trade.
newsitem.headline: EU veto rule blamed for Danish move on Cuba trade.

text.p: European Commission President Jacques Santer on Wednesday used Denmark's decision to block European Union moves on U.S. anti-Cuba laws to call for an end to the use of vetoes in EU decision making.
"This is a very concrete example which shows that...we have to take decisions quickly without unanimity," Santer's spokesman quoted him as saying.
Denmark has said it will veto plans by the EU to agree retaliatory action against America's Helms-Burton legislation, an amalgam of decades of anti-Cuba laws.

Although generally supporting EU objections to the law -- which could impose restrictions on European firms doing business with Havana -- Denmark is concerned that the laws violate individual EU members' sovereignty.
The issue of whether single EU countries should be able to veto EU decisions is one of the most controversial being discussed by negotiators on a new EU treaty.
Most countries say that with the EU set to expand into eastern Europe and the Mediterranean, it is essential that the bloc moves to more majority voting.
Britain, concerned for its sovereignty, has vowed to block any watering down of the veto. Other EU countries also want to retain the veto in specific areas such as taxation and foreign policy.
Until Denmark's decision, the EU had been triumphant over the rare unanimity it had achieved in opposing the Helms-Burton law. The bloc often finds itself divided over external affairs.
The Commission, the EU's executive, believes getting rid of the veto is a step towards having the EU speak abroad with a single voice.
"It is important that we remain credible at an international level," Santer's spokesman said.
